notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on internal relocation and Article 8 remittal.

enrichment.short_title: Kosovo asylum appeal partly allowed on Article 8 mental-health remittal after AE and FE
key_facts: Mr Januzi, an ethnic Albanian from Mitrovica, claimed asylum in the UK on the basis of persecution and later relied on psychiatric evidence that return to any part of Kosovo would risk severe depression and suicide.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal held it would not be unduly harsh to relocate him to Pristina and rejected his Article 3 and Article 8 arguments.
The Secretary of State accepted he could avoid persecution in Pristina, but Dr Barrett's evidence indicated inadequate mental health treatment throughout Kosovo.
The Court of Appeal applied AE and FE v SSHD on the limited comparison required for internal relocation under the Refugee Convention.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination allowing the Secretary of State's appeal against an adjudicator.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part only; IAT order set aside and case remitted to the IAT to determine afresh whether return to Kosovo/Pristina would breach Article 8; Refugee Convention claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: Under AE and FE, reasonableness of internal relocation for refugee status turns on a comparison between conditions in the area of feared persecution and the proposed safe haven, not on conditions in the UK; pan-country disadvantages such as psychiatric care apply equally in both places and are neutral for Refugee Convention purposes, but Article 8 may still be engaged where return would materially worsen mental health compared with treatment in the removing state.
legal_issues: Whether internal relocation to Pristina was unduly harsh under Robinson/AE and FE
Whether return would breach Article 3
Whether the IAT adequately applied Razgar principles on Article 8 and expulsion affecting private life/mental integrity

notes: Complete Chancery judgment on jurisdiction, service out and interim relief in shareholders dispute.

enrichment.short_title: English jurisdiction largely set aside in Maltese tech investment dispute save funding-breach claim
key_facts: Bank of America, Deutsche Bank and UBS investment vehicles invested in iWORLD Group Europe Holdings Ltd, a Maltese technology company founded by Andreas Gerdes and others.
A Shareholders' Agreement governed by English law contained a non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause.
After corporate governance breakdown and disputed transfers of trust-held shares to Medfinco Ltd, the claimants sought wide injunctive relief and permission to serve proceedings in England.
Parallel proceedings were pending in Malta, including appointment of a Board of Administration for the company.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court applications to set aside permission to serve out of the jurisdiction and for interim injunctions, following without-notice ex parte permission.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to serve out set aside except for alleged breach of contractual funding limits against the company; interim injunctions refused in both original and modified form; matter adjourned on service issues with expedited trial contemplated.
enrichment.ratio: A non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause in a contract governed by English law carries strong weight and normally requires strong grounds to displace, but permission to serve out must match viable contractual causes of action; where most claims overlap with Maltese proceedings or lack merit, jurisdiction should be confined to discrete contractual issues such as breach of funding limits.
legal_issues: Effect of a non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause where parties are not EU-domiciled
Whether service out should stand for all defendants and causes of action
Appropriateness of Mareva-style injunctions pending trial
Whether without-notice application involved material non-disclosure
Waiver, estoppel and acquiescence in relation to alleged breaches

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment restoring Equitable's audit negligence claims for trial.

enrichment.short_title: Equitable Life audit negligence claims restored after strike-out of £multi-billion E&Y claims
key_facts: Equitable Life sued Ernst & Young for negligent audits of 1997-1999 accounts, alleging missing technical provisions and failure to disclose contingent liabilities relating to guaranteed annuity rate litigation.
Equitable claimed it would have pursued an orderly sale and tighter bonus policy if directors had known the true financial position.
Langley J struck out lost sale claims and capped bonus declaration claims at £500 million.
For strike-out purposes negligence was assumed; the dispute concerned whether claims were legally or factually hopeless.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from Commercial Court strike-out and case-management orders on pleadings in a professional negligence action.
enrichment.outcome: Equitable's appeal allowed in part; lost sale claims restored but must be pleaded as loss of a chance of sale; bonus declaration claims restored in full subject to extension to about January 2001; E&Y's appeal and cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Auditor negligence claims raising scope of duty, causation and loss of a chance in a developing area should not be struck out where the claimant shows a real rather than fanciful prospect of success; lost sale damages should be framed as loss of a chance, and courts should not at a summary stage cap individual heads of claim by slicing quantum where a full trial is still required.
legal_issues: Whether lost sale and bonus declaration claims had no real prospect of success
Correct formulation of lost sale claims as loss of a chance
Whether Equitable suffered any loss from bonus declarations
Scope of auditors' contractual duty of care and causation under SAAMCO principles
Whether the court could limit bonus claims to £500 million at a summary stage

enrichment.short_title: Bank liable for demising disputed land where quiet-enjoyment covenant extended to title paramount
key_facts: Boundary disputes arose between Unit 13 (leased to the Kettells) and Unit 14 (leased to Mrs Brennan) on an industrial estate in Wallasey.
Land Registry plans conflicted; the Bank re-executed a 1995 lease including a disputed strip while Ferry Cars occupied part of the area.
Mrs Brennan obtained rectification and possession; the Kettells' Part 20 claim against the Bank alleged breach of a covenant for quiet enjoyment extending to title paramount.
Side letters addressed vacant possession concerns but did not clearly accept Mrs Brennan's superior title.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from dismissal of the Kettells' Part 20 claim against Royal Bank of Scotland in underlying boundary litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Part 20 claim against the Bank succeeded in principle with damages to be assessed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a lease covenant protects against interruption by title paramount, the lessor cannot escape liability because the tenant knew of third-party occupation unless there is a clear concluded agreement qualifying the covenant; side letters addressing only vacant possession and Ferry Cars' presence did not bind the tenant to accept the true owner's title.
legal_issues: Construction of covenant for quiet enjoyment including interruption by title paramount
Whether side letters qualified the lease covenant
Prospective versus pre-grant defects under Southwark LBC v Tanner
Distinction between covenant for quiet enjoyment and covenant for title

enrichment.short_title: Hotel sale passed river mooring and advertising rights over retained land under section 62
key_facts: The Crouches sold Petersfield House Hotel but retained Robin's Nest and the Noosa Sound riverside plot with moorings used by hotel guests.
The buyer, P & S Platt Ltd, did not exercise its option to purchase Noosa Sound before expiry.
The defendants then obstructed hotel guests' use of moorings and signage on Noosa Sound.
The transfer incorporated Standard Conditions treating the parties as simultaneous transferees, so section 62 applied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Chancery declarations that quasi-easements over retained land passed to the hotel purchaser on transfer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; declarations upheld except for a fishing right; rectification counterclaim not pursued on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: On a transfer of part of land where section 62 is not excluded, continuous and apparent quasi-easements used for the transferred business pass as legal easements if capable of existing as easements; pre-contract negotiations are generally inadmissible to negate section 62 except in rectification, and rights that do not deprive the servient owner of reasonable use may qualify despite reduced privacy or value.
legal_issues: Whether section 62 converted hotel mooring and signage rights into easements
Relevance of parties' common intention and pre-contract negotiations
Whether mooring rights were exclusive possession or valid easements

enrichment.short_title: Bank customer’s development-loss claim summarily dismissed for want of causation and remoteness
key_facts: Mr Mulvenna claimed Royal Bank of Scotland breached a 1995 refinancing agreement by failing promptly to refund excess interest and charges.
He alleged that but for the breach he would have returned to mainstream banking and obtained about £500,000 finance for HMR/PMR property developments.
District Judge Needham refused summary dismissal; HH Judge Maddocks allowed the bank's appeal and struck out the action.
The bank accepted the refund obligation for summary judgment purposes but denied any duty to extend overdraft limits or fund the developments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission from Rix LJ against summary dismissal of a bank customer's breach-of-contract claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; damages claim for lost development profits held unarguable on causation and remoteness.
enrichment.ratio: Damages for breach of a refund agreement cannot rest on assumed voluntary conduct by the contract-breaker outside its obligations; where the claimant remained outside agreed overdraft limits and the bank had only agreed in principle to consider future lending, loss of development profits is too remote and causation fails because damages must be assessed on the basis of the contract actually made, not conduct the bank was free to refuse.
legal_issues: Appropriate use of summary judgment on complex banking disputes
Whether implied terms extended overdraft facilities beyond the facility letter
Causation where subsequent loss depends on non-contractual lending decisions

Application of Lavarack v Woods minimum-performance principle

enrichment.short_title: Nestlé 'Have a Break' mark refused for lack of distinctiveness; ECJ reference on acquired use
key_facts: Nestlé sought to register HAVE A BREAK alone for class 30 goods despite the well-known slogan 'Have a break... Have a Kit Kat'.
A 1976 application for the same phrase had failed; Mars opposed the 1995 application.
The hearing officer and Rimer J held the mark devoid of inherent distinctive character and insufficiently distinctive through use on its own.
Survey evidence showed some public association with Kit Kat but not enough independent trade-mark significance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission from Aldous LJ against refusal of trade mark registration.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on inherent distinctiveness; question referred to the ECJ on whether acquired distinctiveness may arise from use as part of or with another mark; case to be remitted if the ECJ answer is affirmative.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3(1)(b) requires assessment of whether the mark identifies commercial origin for reasonably observant consumers; a common invitation to consume a snack may lack inherent distinctiveness even if not purely descriptive under section 3(1)(c), and whether use of a phrase alongside a composite mark can establish acquired distinctiveness for the phrase alone is a point of Community law suitable for reference.

Relationship between sections 3(1)(b) and 3(1)(c)

enrichment.short_title: Claimant permitted second obstetric expert where defendants had three consultant obstetric witnesses
key_facts: A child with cerebral palsy alleged negligent obstetric care at birth involving a registrar and consultant at Chesterfield Royal Hospital.
Master Ungley limited each side to one obstetric expert at a case management conference.
The defendants would call Dr Downes and Mr Krishnamurthy as witnesses of fact plus one independent obstetric expert.
The claim was valued at about £1.5 million and turned on Bolam standard-of-care issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a case management order restricting expert evidence in a clinical negligence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claimant permitted to call two obstetric experts as an exceptional departure from the usual one-expert-per-specialty rule.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 35.1 restricts expert evidence to what is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings, and while one expert per specialty is the default, the court may permit more where equality of footing and justice require it—especially in high-value professional negligence litigation where two senior clinician witnesses of fact will inevitably give expertise-based justification evidence, leaving a sole claimant expert potentially outnumbered.
legal_issues: Whether a claimant may instruct two experts in the same specialty
Interaction between witnesses of fact and expert witnesses in professional negligence
Application of the overriding objective and proportionality
Distinction between Bolam liability cases and purely factual medical evidence cases

enrichment.short_title: Extended licence under section 86 for pre-1998 sexual offences held not a retrospective penalty

statutes_considered.title: Powers of the Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000

key_facts: The appellant was sentenced to two years' imprisonment for historic indecent assaults against his stepdaughters committed between 1976 and 1982.
The judge imposed an extended licence under section 86 because section 85 did not apply to offences before 30 September 1998.
At historical sentencing, a two-year prisoner would normally have been on licence until the two-thirds point rather than until the end of sentence.
The court adjourned to consider Article 7 with an advocate to the court after upholding the custodial term.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned judgment in the Court of Appeal on the legality of an extended licence order following partial dismissal of a sentence appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on the extended licence point; section 86 held applicable and not contrary to Article 7; R v J.T. treated as per incuriam.
enrichment.ratio: An extended licence under section 86 is a preventive measure relating to the execution and supervision of sentence, not an autonomous heavier penalty for Article 7 purposes; extending licence until the end of the notional sentence for pre-1998 sexual offences does not violate Article 7 even where offences predated the 1991 Act framework.
legal_issues: Whether section 86 creates a heavier retrospective penalty under Article 7
Distinction between penalty and post-sentencing licence conditions
Application of Welch v UK criteria

notes: Complete tax appeal dismissing trading-stock conversion scheme.

enrichment.short_title: Intra-group property transfer held not acquisition as trading stock despite paper profit
key_facts: New Angel Court Ltd, a Hilton/Ladbroke group property dealing subsidiary, bought nine investment properties from fellow group companies in November 1996.
The properties had already been marketed for disposal and would have produced about £68 million capital losses if sold directly.
Internal documents described tax-driven conversion of capital losses into trading losses available for group relief.
The company resold most properties at a modest profit and elected under section 161(3) to treat the historic capital loss as a trading loss.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a stated case from Special Commissioners dismissing the company's corporation tax loss appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Special Commissioners' decision upheld that the properties were not acquired as trading stock.
enrichment.ratio: Section 173/161 allows conversion of a capital loss into a trading loss only where a trading company genuinely acquires property as trading stock; where an intra-group transfer is essentially a tax scheme with no change in the group's realisation strategy and the dealer company merely lends its name to a pre-existing disposal programme, the transaction lacks commercial justification and the assets remain investment properties in substance.
legal_issues: Meaning of trading stock in an intra-group transfer under section 173(1) TCGA 1992
Relevance of fiscal motive versus commercial justification
Whether the transaction should be viewed at group or single-company level
Application of Coates v Arndale Properties and Reed v Nova Securities
